analysis.one_liner: Strips the labor board of its power to prosecute companies that violate labor law.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate labor committee without a single cosponsor and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have removed the National Labor Relations Board's power to file complaints against employers accused of unfair labor practices — such as firing workers for union organizing — and to stop those practices. Instead, individual workers would have had to sue employers in federal court on their own, with the board limited to investigating. It would also have barred the board from issuing rules affecting workers' or employers' rights, confining it to internal housekeeping.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers, particularly those facing labor board enforcement over retaliation, firing, or refusal to bargain. With no public prosecutor on labor cases, a company accused of illegally firing a union supporter would face a single worker footing the cost of federal litigation rather than the federal government. It would also have voided board rules like those governing union election procedures, ending the board's ability to update them.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the NLRB General Counsel's authority to issue and prosecute unfair labor practice complaints before the board, so no public agency would carry labor cases against employers.
Replaces board enforcement with private civil actions: an aggrieved person could sue in federal district court for relief including an injunction, bearing the burden and cost of the case personally.
Strikes the board's power to 'prevent any person from engaging in' unfair labor practices, converting it to a power only to investigate.

Limits the board's rulemaking to its internal functions and prohibits any rules affecting the substantive or procedural rights of employers, employees, or unions, including rules on unfair labor practices and representation elections.

analysis.who_pays: Individual workers, who would lose the federal government as their advocate in labor disputes and would have to fund federal litigation themselves to challenge illegal firings or retaliation. Labor unions would lose the board rules and enforcement actions that shape organizing and bargaining.

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith argument for the bill is that the current system is slow and one-sided: a worker can wait years while the board and administrative judges process a case, and a direct federal lawsuit with injunctions could in theory be faster.

The honest cost is that the bill replaces public enforcement with self-funded private lawsuits. A worker fired for organizing typically lacks the money to litigate in district court, so many violations would simply go unchallenged; the board's own summary of the bill shows it would keep only investigative powers.
The bill would have stripped the board of rulemaking over representation elections, locking in whatever election procedures existed at enactment and preventing future procedural updates.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is presented as streamlining enforcement, but its effect is to dismantle it: the public prosecutor of labor law disappears, and enforcement shifts to individuals who rarely have the resources to sue. Whatever benefit comes from faster private suits is outweighed by the loss of a functioning enforcement system for workplace rights.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate labor committee, which took no further action before Congress ended, so it never came to a vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Lee introduced the bill on September 18, 2014, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No senator cosponsored the bill; the cosponsor list shows zero.
The action history records no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral; the Congress ended January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers and unions came out ahead because a bill that would have removed federal enforcement of labor rights never advanced. Employers who opposed labor board enforcement would have benefited from the bill, not from its death — its death left existing NLRB enforcement intact.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers, who kept existing labor enforcement

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican introduced the bill with zero cosponsors from either party, and the Democratic-led committee it was sent to took no action on it.

industries.industry: Employers facing union organizing or labor board enforcement
industries.note: This bill would have benefited them by eliminating the public prosecutor of labor cases and voiding board rules on elections and unfair labor practices, shifting enforcement costs onto individual workers. Its interests in this bill run against workers' ability to challenge illegal retaliation. Because the bill died, they gained nothing.

Unions rely on NLRB complaint prosecution and rulemaking to protect organizing and bargaining; the bill would have removed both, leaving workers to sue on their own. Its defeat preserved the existing enforcement system.
